To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the viability of human umbilical endothelial cells (HUVES) exposed to citrate-stabilised gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) decreases as the surface area of the nanoparticles per unit volume of the culture medium increases.
the cytotoxicity of gold nanoparticles depends on both the nanoparticle size and dose and that this toxicity is lower when HUVEC are cultivated under flow condition.

(1) HUVEC viability is higher when the cells are subject to a flowing medium, and this is true independently of the presence of nanoparticles; (2) the viability is lower for cells exposed to a higher nanoparticle surface area; (3) the nanoparticle size does not seem to affect the HUVEC survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a microfluidic platform for the study of nanoparticle toxicity on endothelial cells.
the influence of the shear stress and the nanoparticle size on the cytotoxicity of gold nanoparticles.

a better understanding of the effect that the mode of nanoparticle exposure has on the viability of endothelial cell cultures, and the influence that nanoparticle size has on the toxicity of gold nanoparticles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the size of the nanoparticle does not influence the cell viability in our experimental conditions.
the nanoparticle size and surface area are the main parameters that affect the cytotoxicity of gold nanoparticles.
the mode of exposure to nanoparticles has a major influence on the cytotoxic effects observed in HUVECs, and the size of nanoparticles plays a secondary role.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nanoparticle size does not affect cell viability, while shear stress and nanoparticle concentration do.
the nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio and the flow conditions play a key role in determining nanoparticle toxicity.
the nanoparticle size is a key factor for the cytotoxicity of nanoparticles and that the mode of exposure is also important.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the mode of exposure has a strong influence on the nanoparticle toxicity, and that microfluidic devices can be used to screen nanoparticle cytotoxicity in a manner that is more representative of the in vivo situation than static cell culture.
the microfluidic approach is a valid tool for screening toxicity of gold nanoparticles and that the mode of exposure and the shear stress play a role in determining cell viability.
the mode of exposure has to be carefully considered in order to correctly assess nanoparticle toxicity, and that the use of microfluidic devices is a valuable approach to this aim.
